summary: Describes an architecture for describing SNMP management frameworks. It is a standards-track document. It obsoletes RFC 2271 and was replaced by RFC 3411.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP is the protocol network managers use to read and change information on devices such as routers and servers. This RFC sets out the shape of an SNMP system: an engine that handles messages, security and access control, plus the applications that do the work. It also fixes the names and boundaries, so one part of SNMP can be replaced later without rewriting the others.

questions: what are the snmpv3 security levels
subtitle: The blueprint that names the parts of an SNMP management system and says which document defines each part.

tldr.problem: SNMP had grown into several overlapping specifications, and SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c offered no way to protect a management write. There was no shared structure that let one part of SNMP be replaced without replacing the rest.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits an SNMP system into an engine with four subsystems plus separate applications, and fixes the names, interfaces and registries each part must use. Other documents fill in each slot, so a part can move along the standards track on its own.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2571 obsoleted RFC 2271 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 3411, so RFC 3411 carries this architecture today.

sections.title: Goals and Design Decisions
sections.content:
An SNMP management system holds several nodes, each with an SNMP entity running command responder and notification originator applications (traditionally called agents), and at least one SNMP entity running command generator or notification receiver applications (traditionally called a manager). A management protocol carries information between the entities.

The goals are to reuse existing material, to address the need for secure SET support, which the RFC calls the most important deficiency in SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c, to let parts of the architecture move forward separately even without consensus on everything, to keep SNMP simple, to make a minimal implementation cheap to deploy, and to let features be added when large networks need them.

The design decisions follow. Each subsystem is described by abstract service interfaces, and each document is self-contained so that one part of SNMP can change without directly impacting the others. Security and access control parameters must be remotely configurable. Security Models SHOULD protect against modification of information, masquerade, message stream modification and disclosure, but need not protect against denial of service or traffic analysis. The RFC notes that this modularity of specification does not impose requirements on how implementations are built.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says what an SNMP system must contain and what it can leave out. It wants SNMP to stay simple and cheap on small devices, and it wants one piece to be upgradeable without touching the rest. On security, the goal is to stop someone altering a message or pretending to be another manager. It does not try to stop someone simply blocking traffic, because that looks the same as an ordinary network fault.

sections.title: The Document Set
sections.content:
SNMP is described by a set of documents, not by one. The RFC draws the set as a box of layers. At the top sit a document roadmap, an applicability statement and a coexistence and transition document. Below that, message handling is split into transport mappings, message processing and dispatching, and security. Below that, PDU handling is split into protocol operations, applications and access control. The information model covers the structure of management information, textual conventions and conformance statements, and MIB modules may be written in several older formats.

Each document may be replaced or supplemented. The RFC distinguishes a subsystem, an abstract and incomplete specification of a part of a framework, from a model, a specific design of a subsystem detailed enough to implement, and an implementation, an instantiation of a subsystem that conforms to one or more models.

Protocol operations are grouped by what they do. The Read Class retrieves management information, the Write Class modifies it, the Response Class answers a previous request, the Notification Class sends asynchronous notifications and the Internal Class is exchanged between engines. A second grouping separates operations that expect a response, the Confirmed Class, from those that are not acknowledged, the Unconfirmed Class.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is a family of documents, and this RFC says which document is allowed to define what, so that a new document can be added later without breaking the others. It also sorts the protocol messages into groups: reading, writing, answering, sending notifications and internal traffic. A second split says which messages expect an answer and which do not.

sections.title: The SNMP Engine and Its Subsystems
sections.content:
An SNMP entity is an implementation of the architecture: one SNMP engine plus one or more applications. The engine provides services for sending and receiving messages, authenticating and encrypting them, and controlling access to managed objects. It contains four parts: a Dispatcher, a Message Processing Subsystem, a Security Subsystem and an Access Control Subsystem. Each engine has an snmpEngineID, which is the unique identifier of that engine within an administrative domain.

The Dispatcher sends and receives messages, works out the version of each one and hands it to the matching Message Processing Model, and gives applications an abstract way to send and receive PDUs. The Message Processing Subsystem holds one or more Message Processing Models, one per message format, such as the SNMPv3, SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c models. The Security Subsystem holds one or more Security Models, such as the User-Based Security Model, and each Security Model names the threats it protects against and the protocols it uses. The Access Control Subsystem holds one or more Access Control Models, such as the View-Based one, each defining a particular access decision function.

Applications come in five kinds: command generators, command responders, notification originators, notification receivers and proxy forwarders. An entity with command generators or notification receivers has traditionally been called a manager; one with command responders or notification originators has traditionally been called an agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Every SNMP system has an engine and one or more applications. The engine does the network work: it sends and receives messages, works out which message format arrived, checks who sent it and decides whether the operation is allowed. The applications do the work the operator asked for, such as reading a counter or sending an alert.

sections.title: Contexts, Names and Security Levels
sections.content:
The RFC gives three kinds of names. A principal is the person or program on whose behalf a service is provided or processing takes place. A securityName is a human readable string representing a principal, in a model-independent format. A model-dependent security ID is the model-specific representation of that name, such as a community name or a user name.

Management information lives in an SNMP context, a collection of management information accessible by an SNMP entity. The same item of information may exist in more than one context, and a context is always a subset of a single SNMP entity. To identify one item, four things are needed: the contextEngineID of the entity, the contextName, the managed object type and the instance. The RFC's example gives the description of a network interface: the engine identifier, the context name, the object type ifDescr and the instance "1". A scopedPDU is a block of data holding a contextEngineID, a contextName and a PDU.

Every message also carries a securityLevel, one of noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv or authPriv, ordered from least to most protection. All subsystems and applications must supply a securityLevel or abide by the one supplied.
sections.plainLanguage: One device can hold several sets of management data, so each item is identified by the engine that holds it, the context it sits in and the object itself. The RFC also names the person or program a request is made on behalf of, and gives every message one of three protection levels: none, checked but not hidden, or checked and hidden.

sections.title: Abstract Service Interfaces
sections.content:
The RFC lists the primitives that the subsystems use to talk to each other. The Dispatcher offers sendPdu for an application that wants to send a request or notification to another entity, processPdu to hand an incoming request or notification to an application, returnResponsePdu for an application returning a response, and a primitive for registering responsibility for handling PDUs. Each primitive carries the message processing model, the security model, the security name, the security level, the contextEngineID, the contextName, the PDU version and the PDU itself.

The Message Processing Subsystem prepares outgoing messages and extracts data from incoming ones. The Security Subsystem generates a request or notification message, processes an incoming message and generates a response message. Access control decides whether access to a managed object is allowed.

The RFC states that these interfaces are meant to clarify the externally observable behaviour of SNMP entities and are not intended to constrain the structure or organisation of implementations. They should not be read as APIs or as requirements for APIs.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the calls the engine's parts make to each other, such as send a request or pass an incoming request to an application. It says plainly that these describe what an SNMP system does from the outside, and they do not tell implementers how to organise their own code.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The level of security provided is determined by the Security Model and Access Control Model implementations that are used. Applications have access to data which is not secured, and applications SHOULD take reasonable steps to protect that data from disclosure.

The RFC places four responsibilities on whoever buys an implementation. That person must ensure the implementation complies with the rules of the architecture, that the Security and Access Control Models used satisfy the security and access control needs of the organization, that the implementations of the Models and Applications comply with the model and application specifications, and that the implementation protects configuration secrets from inadvertent disclosure.

The document also contains a MIB definition module. None of its objects is writable and the information they hold is not deemed particularly sensitive, but if that information is judged sensitive in a particular environment, access to it should be restricted through appropriately configured Security and Access Control models.
sections.plainLanguage: How much protection you get depends on which security and access control models an implementation uses, so this RFC cannot promise a level of protection on its own. The final check is left to whoever buys the product: they must confirm that the implementation follows these rules, that its models meet the organization's needs, and that its secrets are not exposed.
